title: Manure Type Rather Than Inoculum Governs the Composting Dynamics of Guinea Pig and Pig Manure Inoculated with Lactic Acid Bacteria or Saccharomyces cerevisiae in High-Andean Bins
content: Low-cost inocula are promoted for composting manure in the Ecuadorian highlands, yet evidence separating substrate from inoculum effects is scarce. This study evaluated, in a completely randomised 2 × 2 factorial design with two bins per treatment, the effects of manure type (guinea pig or pig) and inoculum type (yoghurt lactic acid bacteria or Saccharomyces cerevisiae) over 12 weeks at 2622 m above sea level. Laboratory variables were measured in every bin at weeks 0, 6 and 12, and temperature was also analysed as a repeated measure. No variable differed at week 0 (p ≥ 0.155). Guinea pig bins were 2.50 °C warmer at week 6 (95% CI 0.93 to 4.07) and 0.75 °C warmer at week 12 (0.24 to 1.26), although the overall substrate effect in the repeated-measures model was not significant (p = 0.079). At week 12, guinea pig manure had more ash (+3.65 points) and fixed carbon (+4.20 points) and less total carbon (−3.07 points), and the ash balance indicated organic matter losses of 45% and 33% for guinea pig and pig manure, respectively. The inoculum affected only the week 6 microbial count, which was higher with S. cerevisiae. Manure type, rather than inoculum, explained the observed differences.
